narrative:
The 2022 Washington Nationals were always going to be a team in transition. The departure of Max Scherzer, the looming trade of Juan Soto, and the broader teardown of a championship core left Washington fielding one of the youngest and most inexperienced rosters in the National League. The results were predictable on the surface — 55 wins, 107 losses, a 5.00 ERA, and a run differential that told the story of a team overmatched night after night. But the raw record only tells part of the story of a season that contained genuine moments of hope, unexpected heroes, and a glimpse at what the next chapter might look like.

The early months were a disaster in slow motion. Tanner Rainey, tasked with closing games, became the symbol of a bullpen that simply could not protect leads. Back-to-back catastrophic outings in May and June — surrendering key hits to Shohei Ohtani, Anthony Rendon, and others — defined a team that was competitive deep into games only to watch relief pitchers unravel everything. Kyle Finnegan added to the misery with walk-off damage of his own. April and May records of 7-16 and 11-17 confirmed what the underlying numbers suggested: Washington was one of the worst teams in baseball.

The Juan Soto trade in early August, while a gut punch to the fanbase, paradoxically opened a door. The players who arrived in return, combined with a batch of prospects already on the roster, gave the second half a different energy. Joey Meneses emerged from nowhere — a 30-year-old rookie who had spent a decade grinding through the minors — and delivered the season's single most electric moment when he crushed a three-run homer on September 1st to swing a late game the Nationals' way. CJ Abrams, one of the key pieces in the Soto deal, showed flashes of the player he was destined to become. Lane Thomas, Luis Garcia Jr., and Ildemaro Vargas all contributed moments that gave Washington fans something real to hold onto as the losses piled up.

The 2022 Nationals were not a good baseball team, and no honest retelling can make them one. But within the wreckage of a 55-107 season, the final months offered the kind of evidence that rebuilding franchises desperately need: young players stepping up, surprise contributors defying expectations, and a collection of moments that suggested better days ahead. The foundation was being laid, painfully and imperfectly, but it was being laid.

chapters.title: Sinking Fast
chapters.description: The Nationals stumble through April and May with a porous bullpen and a roster clearly overmatched, going a combined 18-33 in the season's first two months.

chapters.title: Chaos in June
chapters.description: June brings a turbulent mix of bullpen meltdowns and unexpected clutch moments, including Maikel Franco's go-ahead homer and a walk-off single from Lane Thomas, as Washington fights to stay competitive despite going 11-16.

chapters.title: Midsummer Misery
chapters.description: The July heat scorches Washington with a brutal 6-19 record, as Tanner Rainey continues to implode in high-leverage spots and the team's limitations are fully exposed.

chapters.title: The Soto Trade and New Blood
chapters.description: Late July and early August mark the seismic Soto trade and the arrival of new faces, with Luis Garcia Jr. and Joey Meneses providing early hope as Washington goes 9-18 in August but shows flickers of a different identity.

chapters.title: Meneses and the Future
chapters.description: The final weeks of the season belong to Joey Meneses, CJ Abrams, and a group of young players who deliver the year's most memorable moments, giving Nationals fans genuine reasons for optimism heading into the offseason.
